title: Extract person info and reshape
prompt:
You have an array of person records with some fields that might be missing. Build a new array where each person is represented as an object with `name`, `age`, and `city` fields.

If a field is missing, include it as `null` in the output.

Keep the original order.
hints: Grab each person from the array and pick out the three fields you need. If a field does not exist, accessing it will not crash — it will just be `null`.
Use `map` to transform each person. Inside the map, build a new object with the three fields: `{name: ..., age: ..., city: ...}`.

You do not need to guard against missing fields. `$.fieldName` will silently return `null` if the field is not there. A typo in your selector will produce a null in the output instead of an error — that is the trap.
solution:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload map {name: $.name, age: $.age, city: $.city}

explanation.approach: Each person in the input is an object with various fields. Your job is to pick exactly three of them and put them in the output in a specific order. `map` transforms each person into the new shape.

snippets.label: The answer
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload map {name: $.name, age: $.age, city: $.city}
snippets.note: Each person becomes an object with exactly three keys, in the order you wrote them. Bob has no `age` field in the input, so it becomes `null` in the output.

snippets.label: What happens when you access a missing field
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{"name": "Alice"}.age
snippets.note: Accessing a field that is not there returns `null`, not an error. This is the trap: a typo in your field name ships silently as a null in the output.

snippets.label: A person missing all three fields
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload map {name: $.name, age: $.age, city: $.city}
snippets.note: Every field access returns null, so you get an object with all nulls. This is not an error — the output is still valid JSON.

snippets.label: What a typo looks like
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload map {name: $.fullName, age: $.age, city: $.city}
snippets.note: `$.fullName` does not exist, so it becomes null. No compilation error, no warning — the mapping just silently drops the name. This is why the first hint says a typo ships silently.

snippets.label: Order is preserved
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload map {city: $.city, name: $.name, age: $.age}
snippets.note: The output keys appear in the order you wrote them, not the order they appeared in the input. `city` first, then `name`, then `age`.

title: Number each item in a list
prompt:
You have an array of item names. For each item, build an object with two fields: `position` (starting from 1, not 0) and `item`.

Keep the original order.
hints: `map` gives you access to two things at once: the element (`$`) and its index (`$$`). You need both.
The index is zero-based, but the task asks for one-based positions. So index 0 becomes position 1, index 1 becomes position 2, and so on.
Inside your map, return an object with `position: $$ + 1` (to adjust from zero-based to one-based) and `item: $` (the element itself).
solution:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload map {position: $$ + 1, item: $}

explanation.approach: When you map over an array, you have access to the current element (via `$`) and its position in the array (via `$$`). The position is zero-based by default, so you add 1 to get a human-friendly one-based count. Build an object with both pieces of information.

snippets.label: The answer
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload map {position: $$ + 1, item: $}
snippets.note: `$` is the element, `$$` is the index. Index 0 becomes position 1, index 1 becomes position 2, and so on.

snippets.label: What $$ actually is
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload map $$
snippets.note: `$$` is zero-based. The first element is at index 0, the second at index 1, and so on.

snippets.label: The zero-based mistake
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload map {position: $$, item: $}
snippets.note: Forgetting to add 1 gives you zero-based positions. It is valid DataWeave, but it does not answer the task.

snippets.label: What happens if you only use $ without the index
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload map {item: $}
snippets.note: You lose the position information entirely. `map` does not automatically include it; you have to ask for it with `$$`.

snippets.label: The long form with named parameters
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload map ((element, index) -> {position: index + 1, item: element})
snippets.note: Instead of `$` and `$$`, you can name your parameters. The second parameter is the index, the first is the element. Identical result.

title: Active customers only
prompt:
A CRM export gives you an array of customers. Return an **array of the names** of the customers whose `status` is exactly `"active"`.

Some records have no `status` field at all. Those are not active.

Keep the original order.
hints: Two steps, and they chain left to right: narrow the array first, then take one field from each element that is left.
`$` is the current element inside both `filter` and `map`, so `$.status` and `$.name` are all you need.
You do not have to guard against the missing `status`. Ask yourself what `null == "active"` evaluates to.
solution:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload filter ($.status == "active") map $.name

explanation.approach: Two independent jobs — decide *which* records survive, and decide *what* each surviving record becomes. `filter` does the first, `map` does the second, and chaining them left to right reads in the order you thought of them.

snippets.label: The answer
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload filter ($.status == "active") map $.name
snippets.note: `filter` keeps elements, `map` replaces them. Reading it aloud gives you the sentence in the task.

snippets.label: Why the missing field needs no guard
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
null == "active"
snippets.note: `Cy` has no `status`, so `$.status` is `null` — a missing key is null, not an error. Comparing null to a string is simply false, so the record drops out on its own. An `if ($.status != null and ...)` guard would be dead weight.

snippets.label: The tempting alternative, and what it actually returns
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload map (if ($.status == "active") $.name else null)
snippets.note: `map` always returns one element per input element — it cannot drop anything. The rejected rows come back as nulls and the array is still length 3. This is the single most common way this task is got wrong.

snippets.label: The long form, if the shorthand is not comfortable yet
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload filter ((c) -> c.status == "active") map ((c) -> c.name)
snippets.note: Identical result. Naming the parameter is worth it once the lambdas nest and two `$`s would mean two different things.

snippets.label: What happens if the selector is wrong
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload.customers filter ($.status == "active")
snippets.note: Worth seeing once. `payload.customers` does not exist here, and filtering null gives null rather than an error — so a mistyped selector produces an empty-looking result instead of a stack trace. Every array function behaves this way.

title: Apply defaults, but keep false and empty strings
prompt:
A configuration object has some fields that are `null` and need fallback values. Apply defaults for the `timeout`, `retries`, and `debug` fields.

But be careful: if a field has the value `false` or an empty string `""`, those are valid values and should not be replaced. Only `null` gets a default.

Return the updated object with all three fields present.
hints: The `default` operator replaces only `null` values. If a field is missing, the selector returns `null`, so `default` handles both cases in one go.
`false` is a value, not a missing value. The same goes for empty strings: `'' default 'fallback'` keeps the empty string, not the fallback.
Apply `default` to each field selector: `$.timeout default 30`, `$.retries default 3`, and `$.debug default false`.
solution:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{timeout: payload.timeout default 30, retries: payload.retries default 3, debug: payload.debug default false}

explanation.approach: `default` is the right tool for this job. It checks if a value is `null` and replaces it with a fallback. Other falsy values like `false`, `0`, and empty strings are NOT null, so they pass through unchanged. Build an object with three fields, each using `default` to supply its fallback.

snippets.label: The answer
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{timeout: payload.timeout default 30, retries: payload.retries default 3, debug: payload.debug default false}
snippets.note: All three fields are null, so all three defaults kick in.

snippets.label: null gets the default
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
null default 'fallback'
snippets.note: `null` is the ONE case where `default` fires.

snippets.label: false is NOT null
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
false default true
snippets.note: `false` is a value. It is not null, so the default is ignored. `false` passes through.

snippets.label: empty string is NOT null
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
"" default "fallback"
snippets.note: Empty string is a valid value, not null. The default does not apply. This is the trap: many languages treat empty strings as falsy, but DataWeave treats them as real values.

snippets.label: zero is NOT null
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
0 default 3
snippets.note: Zero is a number value, not null. It passes through.

snippets.label: Missing field becomes null, then gets the default
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{timeout: payload.missing default 30}
snippets.note: A field that does not exist returns `null` when accessed, so `default` treats it the same as an explicit `null`.

title: Format a list of names
prompt:
You have a list of names that is formatted as a single string with a pipe separator. The names have extra spaces and are in different cases. Clean them up: trim the spaces, convert to title case (first letter uppercase, rest lowercase), and return them as a newline-separated string.

Title case formula: take the first character, uppercase it, concatenate the rest of the string in lowercase. In DataWeave, a string is an array: `s[0]` is the first character and `s[1 to -1]` is the rest.

For the sample, input `" alice | BOB | Carol "` should produce `Alice\nBob\nCarol`.
hints: Split the string on pipes to get individual names, then transform each one, then rejoin.
You need to trim() each name to remove spaces, then apply title case logic. Title case is: first letter uppercase, the rest lowercase.
You already have a function that takes the first character, uppercases it, and appends the rest in lowercase. Look for a function that does title-casing in one step.
solution:
%dw 2.0
output text/plain
---
payload splitBy "|" map (do { var n = trim($) --- upper(n[0]) ++ lower(n[1 to -1]) }) joinBy "\n"

explanation.approach: Three chained operations: split on the separator, transform each element, join with the output separator. The trap is remembering that splitBy keeps the spaces in each name — each element needs trimming before capitalization.

snippets.label: The answer
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output text/plain
---
payload splitBy "|" map (do { var n = trim($) --- upper(n[0]) ++ lower(n[1 to -1]) }) joinBy "\n"
snippets.note: splitBy breaks on pipes; map transforms each (trim first, then build title case: first letter uppercase, rest lowercase); joinBy reassembles with newlines. The `do { var n = ... }` inside map lets you name the trimmed string so you can split it.

snippets.label: What splitBy actually produces
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload splitBy "|"
snippets.note: The spaces are still there. Each element keeps its surrounding whitespace. Without trim(), the first character of " alice " would be processed, which is a space.

snippets.label: The wrong way: forgetting to trim
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output text/plain
---
payload splitBy "|" map (upper($[0]) ++ lower($[1 to -1])) joinBy "\n"
snippets.note: Without trim(), each name still has its spaces. When you apply the formula to " alice ", the first char is a space and the rest is "alice ", so you get space + lowercase(alice ), which gives " alice ". The spaces are untouched.

snippets.label: String slicing: characters as array indices
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{first: "hello"[0], rest: "hello"[1 to -1]}
snippets.note: [0] gets the first character, [1 to -1] gets from index 1 to the last. So for a string `n`, the formula is always upper(n[0]) ++ lower(n[1 to -1]).

snippets.label: trim() behavior
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{untrimmed: " hello ", trimmed: trim(" hello ")}
snippets.note: trim() removes whitespace from both ends. It does not affect spaces inside the word.

snippets.label: The pipe separator behavior
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
"a|b|c" splitBy "|"
snippets.note: The pipe is literal, not regex. A pipe is just a character, so `splitBy "|"` means 'split on this exact string'.

snippets.label: joinBy assembles back
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output text/plain
---
["Line1", "Line2", "Line3"] joinBy "\n"
snippets.note: The newline literal `\n` produces actual newlines in the output, not the characters backslash and n.

title: Sum prices and round correctly
prompt:
You have a list of prices that may have cents. Calculate the total and round it to the nearest dollar. Use mathematical rounding (0.5 rounds up).

For the sample, the prices `[10.2, 15.75, 8.33]` total to `34.28`, which rounds to `34`.
hints: Two steps: sum all the prices, then round the result to the nearest whole number.
`sum` returns a single number from a list. `round` takes a number and returns it rounded to the nearest integer.
Test: what does `7 / 2` return in DataWeave? Is it a whole number or a decimal? And what does `round` do to that result?
solution:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
round(sum(payload))

explanation.approach: Sum turns an array of numbers into one number. Round then adjusts that number to the nearest integer. The trap is that division in DataWeave always produces decimals — `7 / 2` is `3.5`, not `3`. Formatting with `#` does not round it either.

snippets.label: The answer
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
round(sum([10.2, 15.75, 8.33]))
snippets.note: sum gives 34.28, round gives 34. The chaining is left-to-right: sum fires first, then round.

snippets.label: What sum alone returns
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
sum([10.2, 15.75, 8.33])
snippets.note: Without rounding, you get the exact total with all decimal places. For money, this is usually wrong — you need a whole dollar amount.

snippets.label: Division is never integer division
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
7 / 2
snippets.note: Even with two whole numbers, division produces a decimal. If you want truncation, use floor. If you want rounding, use round.

snippets.label: Formatting with # does not round
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
(7 / 2) as Number {format: '#'}
snippets.note: The format string controls how the number is displayed, not its value. This still returns 3.5 even with the '#' format.

snippets.label: floor vs ceil vs round
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{val: 5.5, floored: floor(5.5), ceiled: ceil(5.5), rounded: round(5.5)}
snippets.note: floor always goes down, ceil always goes up, round goes to the nearest integer (0.5 rounds up).

snippets.label: Why this matters for money
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
sum([0.1, 0.2, 0.3])
snippets.note: DataWeave uses arbitrary-precision arithmetic, so 0.1 + 0.2 + 0.3 is exactly 0.6. But if you use the result in a price list, you need it rounded to cents, which is round(...) for dollars.

title: Extract first and last items
prompt:
You have a list of items. Return an object with `first` and `last` fields containing the first and last items from the list.

For the sample, `["apple", "banana", "cherry"]` should produce `{"first": "apple", "last": "cherry"}`.
hints: Two fields: `first` is payload[0], and `last` is... the last item. In DataWeave, negative indices count from the end.
The last item is at index -1. You do not need to calculate the size; just use the negative index directly.
Think about what happens if the array is empty: payload[0] would be null, and payload[-1] would also be null. That is actually correct behavior for this task.
solution:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{first: payload[0], last: payload[-1]}

explanation.approach: Index the first element with [0] and the last with [-1]. Negative indices count backward from the end, so -1 is always the last item. You do not need to know the array length.

snippets.label: The answer
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{first: ["apple", "banana", "cherry"][0], last: ["apple", "banana", "cherry"][-1]}
snippets.note: Index [0] is the first item, [-1] is the last. No size calculation needed.

snippets.label: Negative indexing: -1 is the last
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
[1,2,3][-1]
snippets.note: Negative indices count from the end. -1 is the last, -2 is second-to-last, etc.

snippets.label: An index past the end is null
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
[1,2,3][9]
snippets.note: Out-of-bounds access does not throw an error; it just returns null. This is useful for defensive coding.

snippets.label: A range is different from an index
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{single: [1,2,3][0], range: [1,2,3][0 to 0]}
snippets.note: [0] returns the item itself, [0 to 0] returns an array with one item. For this task, you want [0] and [-1], not ranges.

snippets.label: sizeOf tells you the length
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{array: [10, 20, 30, 40], size: sizeOf([10, 20, 30, 40])}
snippets.note: sizeOf returns the count. But for the last item, negative indexing is simpler than calculating sizeOf(payload) - 1.

snippets.label: Why the tempting alternative is wrong
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{direct: [1,2,3][-1], calc: [1,2,3][sizeOf([1,2,3]) - 1]}
snippets.note: Both return the same value, but negative indexing is clearer — it says 'get the last' without asking you to do arithmetic.

snippets.label: There is no negative zero
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{ zero: [1,2,3][0], negZero: [1,2,3][-0], negOne: [1,2,3][-1] }
snippets.note: Counting back from the end starts at -1, not -0, because -0 and 0 are the same number. So `[-0]` quietly gives you the FIRST element — the one place where reaching for the end lands you at the start.

title: Combine and delete from lists
prompt:
You are given an array of numbers, then two more arrays.

Combine your first array with the second array. Then remove any elements that appear in the third array.

Return the final array.
hints: Two operators in sequence. `++` comes first, then `--`. Read the inputs as `payload.first`, `payload.second`, `payload.remove`.
`++` glues two arrays into one. `--` removes elements that appear in the second array.
Both operators expect arrays on both sides. Nothing is converted for you — if you have the structure right, it just works.
solution:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload.first ++ payload.second -- payload.remove

explanation.approach: `++` and `--` are binary operators that work left to right. First, concatenate the two arrays. Then, filter out the unwanted elements. The order matters because you are removing from the combined result, not from the parts.

snippets.label: The answer
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload.first ++ payload.second -- payload.remove
snippets.note: Merge first, remove second. The 2 in `first` was part of the merge, so it is there to be removed.

snippets.label: Why order matters
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
(payload.first -- payload.remove) ++ payload.second
snippets.note: Same input, same answer — but only by luck. If the item to remove was in `second`, this version would keep it. The wrong order hides when the trap applies.

snippets.label: Both operands are required to be arrays
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
[1, 2] ++ [3, 4]
snippets.note: `++` joins the right array into the left. Both must be arrays — scalar values are not auto-wrapped.

snippets.label: Remove an element that appears twice
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
[1, 2, 2, 3] -- [2]
snippets.note: `--` removes all instances of each element in the second array, not just the first.

snippets.label: The wrong-order case that reveals the trap
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
(payload.first -- payload.remove) ++ payload.second
snippets.note: Remove from `first` first, then merge. But `second` contains 2, which should have been removed — it comes back in the merge. The right answer filters the final result: `[1] ++ [2] -- [2] -> []`.

title: How many orders at each priority
prompt:
You are given an array of orders, each with a numeric `priority`.

Return **one object** whose keys are the priorities that appear, and whose values are how many orders had that priority.

A priority that never appears must not appear in the output.
hints: One function puts the orders into buckets. Look at what it hands back before you try to count anything — it is not an array.
Counting the members of each bucket is `sizeOf`.
To rebuild an object from an object, `mapObject` gives you the value as `$` and the key as `$$`. A computed key needs parentheses: `($$): ...`
solution:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload groupBy $.priority mapObject { ($$): sizeOf($) }

explanation.approach: `groupBy` does the hard part; the work left over is entirely about the shape it returns. It gives you an **object** — bucket key to array of members — so the second step has to be an object function, not an array one.

snippets.label: Look at what groupBy returns first
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload groupBy $.priority
snippets.note: Two things to notice. It is an object, not an array. And the keys are the strings `"1"` and `"2"` even though `priority` was a number — an object key is always a name, so the grouping value is coerced on the way in.

snippets.label: The answer
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload groupBy $.priority mapObject { ($$): sizeOf($) }
snippets.note: Inside `mapObject`, `$` is the value (the bucket) and `$$` is the key. The parentheses around `$$` are what make it a computed key rather than a field literally named `$$`.

snippets.label: Why not map
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
(payload groupBy $.priority) map sizeOf($)
snippets.note: It does not quietly do the wrong thing — the engine refuses, because `map` has no overload for an Object. This is the good case: the mistake is caught at the point you make it.

snippets.label: The named-parameter form
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload groupBy $.priority mapObject ((orders, priority) -> { (priority): sizeOf(orders) })
snippets.note: Same result. Note the order: **value first, then key**, which is the opposite of how 'key-value' reads. Getting this backwards is a common source of confusion, and because both are often Strings it may not fail — it just produces nonsense.

snippets.label: If you want counts as an array of rows instead
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload groupBy $.priority pluck ((orders, priority) -> { priority: priority, count: sizeOf(orders) })
snippets.note: `pluck` is `mapObject`'s sibling that returns an array. Not what this task asked for, but it is the shape you usually want for a report or a CSV — and see that `priority` has come back out as a String, because that is what it became when it was a key.

title: Total up a numeric field across items
prompt:
You are given an array of objects, each with a numeric `amount` field.

Return the **total** of all amounts.

When the array is empty, your total must be 0, not null.
hints: The `reduce` function combines multiple values into a single result. It takes the element being processed and an accumulator that carries the total forward.
The seed is the starting value for your accumulator. If you do not provide one, an empty array returns null instead of your default.
The parameter order in reduce is `(element, accumulator) -> newAccumulator`. See `reduce` take a look at how the lambda's parameters are ordered.
solution:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload reduce ((item, total = 0) -> total + item.amount)

explanation.approach: `reduce` walks an array one element at a time, passing the current element and the accumulated result to a function. The seed is the starting value — with no seed, an empty array gives null, which is not a number and causes arithmetic to fail.

snippets.label: How reduce processes elements
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
[10, 20, 30] reduce ((element, acc = 0) -> acc + element)
snippets.note: Each element gets added to `acc`, which starts at 0. After the first pass, acc is 10. After the second, 30. After the third, 60.

snippets.label: Extracting a field first
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload reduce ((item, total = 0) -> total + item.amount)
snippets.note: The same technique, but starting with objects. You extract `item.amount` for each and add it to the running total.

snippets.label: Without a seed, empty means null
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
[] reduce ((item, total) -> total + item)
snippets.note: With no seed, reducing an empty array gives null. On non-empty arrays this would fail at runtime when trying to add null, but on an empty array it simply returns null.

snippets.label: The seed as a default value
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
[] reduce ((item, total = 0) -> total + item)
snippets.note: With `total = 0` as the seed, an empty array returns 0. It works with the objects too: the first element arrives at the function with `total` already 0.

snippets.label: The alternative: sum function
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
sum(payload map $.amount)
snippets.note: An alternative path: extract the amounts into an array, then pass it to `sum`. `sum` also returns 0 for an empty array, but `reduce` gives you more control over each step.

title: Iterate over an object's keys and values
prompt:
You are given an object where each key is a product ID and the value is the price.

Return an **array** of objects, one per product, each with `id` and `price` fields.

Arithmetic will coerce a String for you. Comparison will not: it compares text, and as text, "9" comes after "25.50".

{

}

output application/json
---
payload map typeOf($.amount)

%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
sum(payload map $.amount)

%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
max(payload map $.amount)

%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
(payload orderBy $.amount) map $.amount

%dw 2.0

---
{ sumBoth: sum(payload map ($.amount as Number)), maxBoth: max(payload map ($.amount as Number)) }

prompt:

hints: Subtracting one date from another works. Look at what the result *is* before trying to turn it into a number.
The result is a Period, and a Period has parts you can select.
There is a `between` function in `dw::core::Periods` that looks like exactly what you want. Try it, and check its answer against the sample — the two do not agree.
solution:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload map {
  id: $.id,
  days: (($.end as Date) - ($.start as Date)).days
}

explanation.approach: DataWeave gives you two different subtractions between dates, and they mean different things. One produces a **duration** — an elapsed amount of time. The other produces a **calendar period** — years, months and days, the way a person reads a gap off a calendar. The task asks for whole days, which is the first one. Reaching for the function whose name matches the question gets you the second.

snippets.note: Not a number — a Period, printed as `PT672H`. It is an elapsed duration held in hours, and 672 hours is 28 days. This is why the answer cannot just be `end - start`.

snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
(|2027-03-01| - |2027-02-01|).days

%dw 2.0
import * from dw::core::Periods
output application/json
---
{
  period: between(|2027-03-01|, |2027-02-01|),
  days: between(|2027-03-01|, |2027-02-01|).days
}

output application/json
---
payload map { id: $.id, days: ($.end - $.start).days }

title: Triage a queue of retrying jobs
prompt:
A queue of background jobs, each with an `id` and a `retries` count. The record is not always clean: `retries` might be a number (attempts so far), `null` (never attempted), or something else entirely if the record is corrupted (a string, a boolean, an object, ...).

Return an array of `{ id, status }`, where `status` is:

- `"NEW"` if `retries` is `null`
- `"ESCALATE"` if `retries` is a number `>= 3`
- `"RETRYING"` if `retries` is any other number
- `"INVALID"` for anything else
hints: `match` tries its cases top to bottom and stops at the first one that fits. If two cases could both apply to the same value, the one listed first is the one that runs.

A case can test a type with `is`, or test a condition with `if`, but not both at once on the same case — `case n is Number if (n >= 3)` does not compile. Put the type check inside the guard's condition instead, with `and`.
Whichever case tests only `is Number`, with nothing else, will catch every number that reaches it — including the ones a later, more specific case was written for.

explanation.approach: `match` is tried top to bottom and stops at the first case that fits — it is not "find the most specific case", it is "find the first one". A case can test a type with `is Type`, or test an arbitrary condition with `if (...)`, but DataWeave does not let a single case do both at once; `case n is Number if (n >= 3)` is a compile error, not a stricter case. To get both a type check and a threshold on the same branch, the type check has to move inside the guard's own condition with `and`. Once that branch exists, it has to be listed before the plain `is Number` case — a bare `is Number` case placed first will catch every number, including the ones the guarded case further down was written to catch, and that guarded case becomes unreachable code that never causes an error and never runs.

snippets.label: A case cannot combine `is Type` and a guard
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
10 match {
  case n is Number if (n >= 3) -> "escalate"
  else -> "other"
}
snippets.note: This is not "Number, and also at least 3" — it simply does not compile. The type test and the guard cannot live on the same case.

snippets.label: The threshold has to go inside the guard's condition instead
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
10 match {
  case n if (n is Number and n >= 3) -> "big"
  case n is Number -> "num"
  else -> "other"
}
snippets.note: `is` works fine as a plain boolean check inside a guard's `(...)`. Listed first, this guard gets a chance to run before the broader `is Number` case below it.

snippets.label: Swap the order and the guard goes dead
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
10 match {
  case n is Number -> "num"
  case n if (n >= 3) -> "big"
  else -> "other"
}
snippets.note: Same two cases, reversed order. `10` satisfies both, but `match` stops at the first fit — `case n is Number` — so the guarded case below it never runs, for any number at all, not just this one.

snippets.label: `null` gets its own case, not `is Number`
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
null match {
  case n is Number -> "num"
  case null -> "isNull"
  else -> "other"
}
snippets.note: `null` is matched with the literal `case null`, and it has to come before `else` or it would fall into that instead.

snippets.label: Everything else falls to `else`
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
true match {
  case n is Number -> "num"
  case null -> "isNull"
  else -> "other"
}
snippets.note: A Boolean matches none of the specific cases, so it lands on `else` — this is where a corrupted `retries` field (a string, a boolean, an object) ends up as `INVALID`.

title: Flag repeat webhook deliveries
prompt:
A webhook provider delivers at least once, so the same event can show up more than once in a batch. Deliveries arrive in the order they were received, each with an `eventId`.

Return each delivery with a `duplicate` field added: `true` if the same `eventId` already appeared **earlier** in the batch, `false` if this is that event's first delivery. Only look backward — a later repeat does not make the first delivery a duplicate.
hints: You need to know what happened at every position before this one — not whether the `eventId` appears anywhere in the whole batch.
`map` can hand you the index of the current element as a second parameter. A `do` block right there lets you name the slice of the array that comes before that index, without writing the slice twice.

A `var` declared in the header runs once, before the `map` starts, and has no idea which element is currently being looked at — it cannot hold 'everyone seen so far' the way a mutable loop variable would. The 'seen so far' slice has to be recomputed inside the map, for every element.

explanation.approach: DataWeave has no mutable loop state: a `var` declared in the header is computed exactly once, before the `map` runs at all, and a `do` block placed inside the `map` runs fresh for every element, with no memory of what earlier elements did. There is no way to build up a running 'seen so far' list by declaring it once in the header. The correct approach instead recomputes, for each element, which elements came before it by index, and checks membership only against that earlier slice. A version that asks 'does this eventId appear anywhere in the whole payload' cannot tell first occurrence from repeat, since from that question's point of view they look identical.

snippets.label: A header var never sees what happens per element
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
var seenSoFar = []
---
payload map (delivery) -> delivery ++ { seenSoFar: seenSoFar }
snippets.note: `seenSoFar` is computed once, before the map starts, and every element gets back the exact same empty value. A header var cannot accumulate anything as a map goes along — there is no hidden mutable state to update.

snippets.label: `$$` — and the slice built from it — only exists inside the map
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
var x = $$
---
x
snippets.note: The index is not available at the header at all, which is why 'everyone before this element' cannot be hoisted out of the `map` — it has no `$$` to slice from up there.

snippets.label: The correct shape: recompute the earlier slice per element
snippets.note: Each element gets its own fresh `priorIds`, built from only the part of the array before its own index.

snippets.label: Checking the whole list instead of just what came before
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload map (delivery) -> delivery ++ { duplicate: (sizeOf(payload filter ($.eventId == delivery.eventId))) > 1 }
snippets.note: The very first `E1` is now marked a duplicate, because this check can already see the second `E1` that has not been delivered yet from that record's own position in the list.

snippets.label: A range ending in `-1` means 'to the last element', not 'to nothing'
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
[1,2,3][0 to -1]
snippets.note: This is why the first element needs an explicit `if (idx == 0) []` instead of trusting `payload[0 to idx - 1]` to come out empty on its own — at `idx = 0` that range is `[0 to -1]`, which is the whole array, not an empty one.

title: Sum every number, however deep it is buried
prompt: A payload can nest objects inside arrays inside objects, to any depth, and the depth is not known ahead of time. Write `sumAll` that adds up every number found anywhere inside the payload, at any level, and ignores anything that isn't a number (strings, booleans, `null`).
starter:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
fun sumAll(v) = v match {
  ???
}
---
sumAll(payload)
hints: You don't know how deep the nesting goes ahead of time, so there's no fixed number of `.a.b.c` selectors that would work on every input — the function has to call itself.

At each call, what you were handed is either an Object, an Array, or a leaf. An Object needs every one of its values visited; an Array needs every one of its items visited; a leaf is either a Number worth keeping or something worth ignoring.

Visiting the values inside an Object is not the same as summing whichever of them happen to be Numbers directly — if one of those values is itself an Object or an Array, it has to go through the same function again, not just get type-checked and skipped.
solution:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
fun sumAll(v) = v match {
  case o is Object -> sum(o pluck ((value) -> sumAll(value)))
  case a is Array -> sum(a map ((item) -> sumAll(item)))
  case n is Number -> n
  else -> 0
}
---
sumAll(payload)

explanation.approach: There's no loop construct that walks arbitrarily deep data on its own, so `sumAll` has to test what it was given at each call — is it an Object, an Array, or a leaf — and for the two container cases, call itself again on every value or item found inside, rather than stopping to inspect them directly. A leaf that isn't a Number contributes 0. A version that checks the type of what's directly inside an Object or Array, without calling `sumAll` again on it, behaves identically to the real thing on data that happens to be only one level deep, and silently returns 0 for anything nested any deeper than that — because a nested Object or Array is neither ignored nor a Number, and this version has no third option beyond those two.

snippets.label: No return-type annotation needed, even though it's recursive
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
fun sumAll(v) = v match {
  case o is Object -> sum(o pluck ((value) -> sumAll(value)))
  case a is Array -> sum(a map ((item) -> sumAll(item)))
  case n is Number -> n
  else -> 0
}
---
sumAll(payload)
snippets.note: `fun sumAll(v) = ...` declares neither the parameter's type nor the return type, and it still compiles and recurses correctly.

snippets.label: Empty containers and non-numeric leaves both contribute zero
snippets.note: `sum` of an empty array is `0`, which is what a container with nothing numeric inside it eventually reduces to.

snippets.label: The wrong version, on the same nested payload
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
fun sumAll(v) = v match {
  case o is Object -> sum(o pluck ((value) -> if (value is Number) value else 0))
  case a is Array -> sum(a map ((item) -> if (item is Number) item else 0))
  else -> 0
}
---
sumAll(payload)
snippets.note: Nothing is directly a Number inside the top-level Object — `a` is an Object and `d` and `e` are not numbers — so this version reports 0 for a payload whose numbers add up to 15. It never looks inside `a`, `e`, or the objects nested further in.

snippets.label: The same wrong version looks correct on flat data
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
fun sumAll(v) = v match {
  case o is Object -> sum(o pluck ((value) -> if (value is Number) value else 0))
  case a is Array -> sum(a map ((item) -> if (item is Number) item else 0))
  else -> 0
}
---
sumAll({"a": 1, "b": 2, "c": 3})
snippets.note: This is exactly why the bug survives a quick check — a flat object has nothing nested inside it to expose the missing recursive call.

snippets.label: Without `else`, an unhandled leaf is a runtime error
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
fun sumAll(v) = v match {
  case o is Object -> sum(o pluck ((value) -> sumAll(value)))
  case a is Array -> sum(a map ((item) -> sumAll(item)))
  case n is Number -> n
}
---
sumAll(payload)
snippets.note: `case n is Number` covers numbers, but nothing covers a String, Boolean, or null leaf — `match` throws rather than falling through to some default.

title: Redact every email address, whatever shape it's hiding in
prompt:
A payload arrives with no fixed shape — some fields are plain, some are nested objects, some are arrays of objects, arrays of arrays, whatever the upstream system felt like sending that day.

Replace every string value that looks like an email address (it contains an `@`) with the literal string `"REDACTED"`, no matter how deeply it is nested. Leave every other value exactly as it is — same value, same type. A number must stay a number and a boolean must stay a boolean in the output; do not turn them into strings along the way.
hints: There is a module built exactly for walking a value of unknown shape and touching every terminal value inside it. It is not in core.
The callback runs once per leaf, however deep the leaf is — one field two levels down, one item inside an array inside an object. Not every leaf that reaches it is a String.

The function reference's own example turns every leaf into a string with `upper(value as String)`. That works there because every leaf in that example happens to already be a string. Check what your callback does to a leaf that is not one.
solution:
%dw 2.0
import * from dw::util::Tree
output application/json
---
payload mapLeafValues ((v, p) -> if ((v is String) and contains(v, '@')) 'REDACTED' else v)

explanation.approach: The payload's shape is not fixed, so a hand-written walk has to correctly recurse into both Objects and Arrays, at every depth, or it silently skips a branch. `dw::util::Tree`'s `mapLeafValues` already does that walk: it calls the callback once for every terminal value in the structure, regardless of whether that value sits inside nested objects, inside arrays, or inside arrays of objects. The task then reduces to one decision per leaf — is this a String that contains `@`? — and the one trap is deciding what to do with everything else: it must come back unchanged, not coerced into a String.

snippets.label: mapLeafValues is not in core
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
mapLeafValues({a:1}, (v,p) -> v)
snippets.note: Without `import * from dw::util::Tree`, the name simply does not resolve — a plain CompilationException, with nothing in the message pointing at the missing import.

snippets.label: The generic walk, on a small fixture
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
import * from dw::util::Tree
output application/json
---
mapLeafValues({a:{b:'x'},c:['y']}, (v,p) -> upper(v as String))
snippets.note: One leaf is two objects deep (`a.b`), the other is inside an array (`c[0]`). Both get the callback. That is the walk this module gives you for free.

snippets.label: Checking the type before matching
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
import * from dw::util::Tree
output application/json
---
{name: "Alice", email: "alice@example.com", age: 30} mapLeafValues ((v, p) -> if ((v is String) and contains(v, '@')) 'REDACTED' else v)
snippets.note: `age` reaches the callback too — every leaf does — but it is not a String, so the `is String` check keeps it as the number `30`, not `"30"`.

snippets.label: Skip the type check and coerce instead, and the numbers quietly become strings
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
import * from dw::util::Tree
output application/json
---
{name: "Alice", email: "alice@example.com", age: 30} mapLeafValues ((v, p) -> if (contains(v as String, '@')) 'REDACTED' else (v as String))
snippets.note: This is the shape of the function reference's own example, applied to data where not every leaf is already a String. `age` is still redacted correctly (30 does not contain `@`), but it comes back as `"30"` — a string in the output where the input had a number.

snippets.label: The walk reaches inside an array of objects two levels down
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
import * from dw::util::Tree
output application/json
---
payload mapLeafValues ((v, p) -> if ((v is String) and contains(v, '@')) 'REDACTED' else v)
snippets.note: Both `lead` fields and both `members` entries are leaves, whether they sit directly in an object or inside an array nested inside that object's array of teams. `mapLeafValues` does not care which.

snippets.label: Why not hand-roll it: a recursive mapObject skips arrays entirely
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
fun redactObj(o: Object): Object = o mapObject ((v, k) -> { (k): if (v is Object) redactObj(v) else if ((v is String) and contains(v, '@')) 'REDACTED' else v })
---
redactObj(payload)
snippets.note: `redactObj` only recurses when a value `is Object`. An Array is neither an Object nor a String, so it falls into the last `else v` and comes back completely untouched — `bob@example.com` survives inside `notes` because nothing ever looked inside that array.

title: Enrich orders with the customer that placed them
prompt:
You are given `payload.orders`, an array of `{ orderId, customerId }`, and `payload.customers`, an array of `{ id, name }`.

Return an array of `{ orderId, customerId, customerName }`, one entry per order, in the order the orders appear.

If an order's `customerId` does not match any customer, `customerName` is `null`. A customer that no order references does not appear in the output at all.
hints: This is a join, not a nested lookup you have to write by hand. `leftJoin` lives in `dw::core::Arrays`, not core — without importing it, the name does not resolve.

`leftJoin` does not merge anything for you. Each element of its result is `{l: <left item>, r: <right item>}` — one item from each side, not a single combined object. You still have to build the shape the question asks for.

When a left item has no match, the result element has no `r` key at all — not `r: null`. Selecting through a missing key still gives you `null`, so `$.r.name` already produces the fallback the question wants, with no extra check needed.
solution:
%dw 2.0
import * from dw::core::Arrays
output application/json
---
leftJoin(payload.orders, payload.customers, (o) -> o.customerId as String, (c) -> c.id as String)
  map { orderId: $.l.orderId, customerId: $.l.customerId, customerName: $.r.name }

explanation.approach: `leftJoin` is not part of core DataWeave — it lives in `dw::core::Arrays` and has to be imported. Its job is narrower than 'give me the merged rows': it walks the left array and, for each item, attaches the right item whose key matches, if one exists. What comes back is a pair, `{l: ..., r: ...}` — one item from each side, never a single merged object — and when nothing on the right matches, the pair simply has no `r` at all rather than `r: null`. Turning that into the shape this question wants, and handling both edges — an order with no customer, and a customer no order points to — is the actual work.

snippets.label: Without the import, the name does not resolve
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
leftJoin([{id:'1'}],[{id:'1'}],(l)->l.id,(r)->r.id)
snippets.note: `leftJoin` is not in core. Calling it without `import * from dw::core::Arrays` is a compile error, not a runtime one.

snippets.label: What leftJoin actually returns: pairs, not merged rows
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
import * from dw::core::Arrays
output application/json
---
leftJoin(payload.orders, payload.customers, (o) -> o.customerId as String, (c) -> c.id as String)
snippets.note: Every element is `{l, r}` — the left order and the matched customer, sitting side by side rather than combined. Building `{ orderId, customerId, customerName }` out of this is a separate step.

snippets.label: An order with no matching customer has no r key at all
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
import * from dw::core::Arrays
output application/json
---
leftJoin([{orderId:'O3',customerId:99}], [{id:1,name:'Ann'}], (o) -> o.customerId as String, (c) -> c.id as String)
snippets.note: Customer 99 does not exist, so the pair for order O3 has an `l` and nothing else — there is no `r` field to be null, it is simply absent.

snippets.label: Selecting through the missing key still gives null
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
import * from dw::core::Arrays
output application/json
---
(leftJoin([{orderId:'O3',customerId:99}], [{id:1,name:'Ann'}], (o) -> o.customerId as String, (c) -> c.id as String))[0].r.name
snippets.note: `.r` is absent, and DataWeave selectors on a missing or null value keep returning null rather than erroring. `$.r.name` already does the right thing for an unmatched order with no extra handling.

snippets.label: The plausible wrong approach: a nested filter per row
snippets.note: This looks reasonable and passes on data where everything matches. But the trailing `filter` that was meant to clean up ends up deleting order O3 entirely, because it has no customer and so no way to tell 'unmatched' apart from 'exclude this row'. The question asked for O3 to appear with `customerName: null` — it just vanished instead.

snippets.label: The full answer
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
import * from dw::core::Arrays
output application/json
---
leftJoin(payload.orders, payload.customers, (o) -> o.customerId as String, (c) -> c.id as String)
  map { orderId: $.l.orderId, customerId: $.l.customerId, customerName: $.r.name }
snippets.note: The join finds the pairs; the `map` afterward flattens each `{l, r}` pair into the final shape, and `$.r.name` reads as null on its own for any order that had no match.

title: Rename every field to its human-readable label
prompt:
You are given `payload.data`, an object of raw values keyed by internal field IDs like `f1`, `f2`, and `payload.labels`, an object mapping some of those same field IDs to human-readable names.

Build a new object with the same values, but with each key replaced by its label. A field ID that has no entry in `labels` keeps its original key.

Two different field IDs can be labeled with the exact same name (two internal fields both meaning "comments", say). When that happens, keep **both** entries in the output under that shared name, in the order they appear in `data` — do not collapse them.
hints: You need to build an object whose keys come from data, not from the script text. `mapObject` walks an object and lets you produce a new one; wrapping an expression in parentheses as a key — `(expr): value` — makes it a computed key, evaluated rather than read literally.

`mapObject` hands its lambda the value, the key, and the position, in that order — value first. The field ID you need for the lookup is the second parameter. To read a field of `labels` whose name you only know at runtime, use a bracket selector like `payload.labels[k]`; when the ID is not present, that gives `null`, and `default` supplies the fallback.

Leaving off the parentheses does not error — it silently changes the meaning. `{ k: v }` builds a field literally named `k` for every entry, not whatever value the variable `k` holds, so you would get the same key repeated for every row instead of the labels you looked up.
solution:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload.data mapObject ((v, k, i) -> { (payload.labels[k] default k): v })

explanation.approach: The new key for each field is not known when the script is written — it depends on looking the field ID up in `labels`. `mapObject` gives you each value and key of `data` in turn; wrapping the looked-up label in parentheses, `(payload.labels[k] default k): v`, makes DataWeave evaluate it into a key rather than treating it as a literal field name. Because DataWeave objects are ordered lists of pairs, two fields that resolve to the same label both survive in the output side by side, instead of the second overwriting the first.

snippets.label: Looking a value up by a key you only know at runtime
snippets.note: A bracket selector with a variable inside it reads the field whose name is the variable's value, not a field literally called `k`.

snippets.label: Without parentheses, the key is the literal word
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
do { var k = 'x' --- { k: 1 } }
snippets.note: Even though `k` holds `'x'`, writing `k:` as a bare key builds a field named `k`. The variable is never read.

snippets.label: With parentheses, the key becomes the variable's value
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
do { var k = 'x' --- { (k): 1 } }
snippets.note: The parentheses are what turn `k` from a field name into an expression to evaluate. This is the whole trick a computed key relies on.

snippets.label: mapObject hands you value first
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload mapObject ((v, k, i) -> { (k): [v, i] })
snippets.note: The lambda's first parameter is the value, the second is the key, and the third is the index — the opposite order from how you would say the pair out loud.

snippets.label: The wrong way: forgetting the parentheses when renaming
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload.data mapObject ((v, k, i) -> { k: v })
snippets.note: Every entry lands under the literal key `k`, because the bare identifier was never turned into an expression. The labels lookup does not even run.

snippets.label: The answer, and why the duplicate label survives
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload.data mapObject ((v, k, i) -> { (payload.labels[k] default k): v })
snippets.note: `f3` and `f7` both resolve to `comments`. DataWeave objects do not deduplicate keys, so both pairs come through in the order they were built.

solution:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
ns soap http://schemas.xmlsoap.org/soap/envelope/
ns cust http://acme.com/customer
ns audit http://acme.com/audit
---
payload.soap#Envelope.soap#Body.cust#GetCustomersResponse.*cust#Customer map {
  id: $.@id,
  name: $.cust#Name,
  status: $.cust#Status
}

explanation.approach: A namespace-qualified element is identified by its local name AND its namespace URI together — the two form one key. But a selector written without a namespace prefix, like `.Status`, only ever asks about the local name. When a document has exactly one element with that local name, the distinction never comes up and the bare selector looks perfectly fine. It only breaks once a second element with the same local name — in a different namespace — enters the document, and it breaks silently: it just returns whichever one appears first, with no error to flag the ambiguity.

snippets.label: Two elements, same local name, different namespaces

---
payload.root.Status
snippets.note: The bare `.Status` selector matches `a:Status` simply because it is the first sibling in the document — not because it belongs to any particular namespace. `b:Status` is silently skipped.

snippets.label: Qualifying both selectors resolves the ambiguity

%dw 2.0

ns b http://b.com
---
{ aStatus: payload.root.a#Status, bStatus: payload.root.b#Status }
snippets.note: Once each selector names both the prefix and the local name, each one reaches exactly the element it means.

title: A total that must add up to the cent
prompt:
You are given an array of transaction amounts, in dollars, as numbers (some negative, for refunds). Return `{ total }`, where `total` is the sum of all the amounts, formatted as a string with exactly two decimal places (for example `"18.00"`, not `"18"`).

Round only once, at the very end, to produce the two-decimal string. Do not round any individual amount before summing — the amounts are exact, and there is nothing to protect them from.
hints: This engine's numbers are exact decimals, not the IEEE doubles of JavaScript or Java — a habit like 'round early to avoid floating-point drift' is solving a problem that does not exist here.
Sum the whole array first, as-is, and only convert the total to a two-decimal string as the very last step.
If you round every amount to cents before summing 'just to be safe', try it on several amounts that each end in .125 — the total changes by a cent from what summing first and rounding once gives you.
solution:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{ total: sum(payload) as String {format: "0.00"} }

explanation.approach: DataWeave numbers are arbitrary-precision decimals, not IEEE 754 doubles. `0.1 + 0.2` really is `0.3` here — there is no accumulated binary rounding error to defend against. The trap runs backwards from what JavaScript or Java teach: a habit of rounding every intermediate amount 'to be safe' is not neutral. `sum` over the exact amounts and `round` (or a string format) applied once at the end give the mathematically correct total; rounding each amount first throws away precision the final answer needed, and the two totals can disagree by real money.

snippets.label: 0.1 + 0.2 is exact here
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{ v: 0.1 + 0.2, eq: (0.1 + 0.2) == 0.3, t: typeOf(0.1 + 0.2) }
snippets.note: No floating-point residue, and the type is still a plain Number. The habit of guarding against `0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3` comes from other languages and does not apply here.

snippets.label: Sum first, round once, at the end
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
sum([10.125, 10.125, 10.125]) as String {format: "0.00"}
snippets.note: The exact sum is 30.375. Formatting it to two decimals in one step rounds it once, giving 30.38.

snippets.label: Rounding each amount to cents first, then summing
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
sum([10.125, 10.125, 10.125] map ((round($ * 100)) / 100)) as String {format: "0.00"}
snippets.note: Each 10.125 rounds up to 10.13 on its own — `round` rounds a `.5` away from zero, and 10.125 * 100 is 1012.5. Three of those sum to 30.39, a cent more than summing the exact amounts and rounding once.

snippets.label: round() on an exact half rounds away from zero
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
[round(0.5), round(1.5), round(2.5), round(-0.5)]
snippets.note: This is why the per-amount rounding above tips 10.125 up to 10.13 instead of down to 10.12 — and why doing it three times, before the sum, is not the same as doing it once, after.

snippets.label: A case where early rounding does not happen to move the total
snippets.note: The two approaches do not always disagree — here the per-amount rounding errors cancel out. That is what makes the habit dangerous: it passes most of the time, and only a specific mix of amounts, like three that each end in .125, exposes the cent it drops or adds.

title: A sales summary, two levels deep
prompt:
You are given an array of sales records, each `{ region, category, amount }`. Build a summary object where each key is a `region`, and each value is an object mapping `category` to the sum of `amount` for that region and category.

For example, two `West` records in `Widgets` and one in `Gadgets` become `{ "West": { "Widgets": <sum>, "Gadgets": <sum> } }`. A region that only ever appears with one category still produces an object, just with one key.
hints: `groupBy` hands you back an Object, keyed by whatever you grouped on — not an Array. Check `typeOf` on the result before deciding what to do with it next.

You need this shape twice: once to bucket by region, and again inside each bucket to bucket by category. Whatever turns an Object into another Object without leaving Object-land is what you want at both levels.
`map` expects an Array. Calling it directly on the result of `groupBy` is not a smaller version of the right answer — it does not run at all.

explanation.approach: `groupBy` never returns an Array — it returns an Object whose keys are the grouping values and whose values are the Arrays of matching items. That means the next step in the chain has to be something that iterates an Object, which is `pluck` (Object to Array) or `mapObject` (Object to Object), never `map` (Array to Array). A two-level report just applies this twice: group by region into an Object of Arrays, then inside each Array group by category and reduce each bucket to a single number with `sum`.

snippets.label: Check the shape before you chain anything onto it
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{ raw: typeOf(payload), grouped: typeOf(payload groupBy $.region) }
snippets.note: An Array goes in and an Object comes out. That one line decides everything after it: the next step has to be an object function, and reaching for `map` here is an error rather than a wrong answer.

snippets.label: What groupBy actually hands back
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload groupBy $.region
snippets.note: An Object, keyed by region, each value still the Array of full records that matched. Nothing has been summed yet.

snippets.label: Calling map on that Object
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
(payload groupBy $.region) map $
snippets.note: `UnexpectedFunctionCallTypesException`: map wants an Array and was handed an Object. This is not a wrong answer that runs — it does not run at all, which is exactly why it is easy to write without noticing: the mistake shows up as a stack trace, not a bad number.

snippets.label: mapObject, going Object to Object, is the shape that fits
snippets.note: This is one level of aggregation — a single total per region. It compiles and runs, but it throws away the category breakdown the report actually needs; West's Widgets and Gadgets are already merged into 140 before there is any chance to split them back out.

snippets.label: The full two-level chain
snippets.note: The inner `groupBy $.category mapObject ...` runs once per region, on that region's own Array of records, before its result becomes the value stored under `(region)`.

snippets.label: pluck is the Object-to-Array alternative, useful for a flatter report
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload groupBy $.region pluck ((lines, region) -> { region: region, total: sum(lines.amount) })
snippets.note: Same grouped Object, but `pluck` turns it into an Array of `{region, total}` rows instead of a nested Object. Neither `pluck` nor `mapObject` is `map` in disguise — each names what the input actually is.

title: Parse a fixed-width payroll extract
prompt:
A mainframe payroll job writes one line per employee, with no delimiters between fields — every field sits at a fixed character position:

| field | start (0-based) | length |
|---|---|---|
| id | 0 | 6 |
| name | 6 | 20 |
| salary | 26 | 10 |
| dept | 36 | 3 |

`name` is space-padded on the right to fill its width. `salary` is zero-padded on the left and always has exactly two decimal digits, for example `0004250.00`. Lines are separated by `\n`, and the file may contain blank lines.

Return an array of `{ id, name, salary, dept }`, one per non-blank line, with `name` and `dept` trimmed and `salary` as a Number.
hints: The payload here is one big String with newlines in it, not a parsed structure — there is no reader doing the work for you. Split it into lines first.

Each field lives at a fixed character position, not behind a delimiter. A range selector like line[6 to 25] on a String pulls out a substring; pair every field with trim, since the padding is real characters, not formatting.

Describe the layout as a list of { name, start, length } and reduce over it per line. Two things bite: a field width that is off by one silently drops or adds a character instead of erroring (it only shows up when a value exactly fills its column), and a blank line in the file is not a record — filter it out before parsing, or it survives the split and fails later at the `as Number` coercion instead of at the split.

explanation.approach: There is no reader for this format here — application/flatfile in this engine requires a schema resource loaded from the classpath, and passing one inline as a reader property does not satisfy it (it fails with 'No schema set' no matter what the property is named). So the file arrives as inputMime text/plain, a single String, and the parsing is manual: split on newlines, then pull each field out of a line with a range selector at a fixed offset. The two ways this goes wrong without an error are a field width that is off by one, and a blank line that survives the split.

snippets.label: The payload is a plain String here, not a parsed structure
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload splitBy "\n"
snippets.note: splitBy on the raw text gives an array of line Strings. Nothing has been parsed into fields yet.

snippets.label: A range selector plus trim pulls one field out
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
trim("E00001Alice Chen          0004250.00ENG"[6 to 25])
snippets.note: line[6 to 25] is the 20-character name column, spaces and all. trim removes the padding — it does not know or care where the padding came from.

snippets.label: A parsed field is still a String until you say otherwise
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{
  raw: "E00001Alice Chen          0004250.00ENG"[26 to 35],
  rawType: typeOf("E00001Alice Chen          0004250.00ENG"[26 to 35]),
  asNumber: "E00001Alice Chen          0004250.00ENG"[26 to 35] as Number
}
snippets.note: The salary column comes out as the String "0004250.00". as Number drops the leading zeros and keeps the cents — 4250, not a display string.

snippets.label: Why application/flatfile is not the answer here
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
read(payload, "application/flatfile", {schema: [ {name: "name", size: 10}, {name: "age", size: 3} ]})
snippets.note: This is the built-in flat-file reader, and it looks like the right tool. It throws IllegalStateException: No schema set regardless of what the schema property is called or shaped — this engine expects the schema as a classpath resource, which a headless practice script has no way to supply. Range selectors on a String are the fallback that actually works.

snippets.label: One column short is silent, not an error
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
var layout = [ { name: "name", start: 6, length: 19 } ]
fun field(line, start, length) = trim(line[start to (start + length - 1)])
---
field("E00002Bartholomew Chen III0001500.75SAL", 6, 19)
snippets.note: r2's name is exactly 20 characters — "Bartholomew Chen III" — with no padding to spare. Reading only 19 of them drops the trailing "I" and returns a different, still-plausible-looking name. No exception, no null — just a wrong answer, and only on the one row with no slack in it.

snippets.label: A blank line fails later than you'd expect
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
("" splitBy "\n") map (line) -> line[26 to 35] as Number
snippets.note: An empty line has no character at position 26 — the selector returns null, and null as Number throws UnsupportedTypeCoercionException. The failure surfaces at the coercion, several steps after the split that actually produced the bad element, which is why filtering blank lines up front is easier than debugging this backward.

title: Embed an order's line items as a CSV attachment
prompt:
Each order is `{ orderId, items }`, where `items` is an array of `{ sku, qty, price }`.

Return an array of `{ orderId, csv, total }`:

- `csv` is the order's line items written out as CSV text, with columns in the order `sku, qty, price` — a String, embedded as one field of the JSON output, not a separate file.
- `total` must be computed by reading that same CSV string back and summing `qty * price` over its rows — not computed straight from `items`.

An order with no items has `csv` as an empty string and `total` of `0`.
hints: `write(value, "application/csv")` does not print anything — it returns a String. Put that String straight into a field of the object you output, the same as any other value.

The columns `write` produces follow the field order of the objects you hand it, not any order tied to the question. If an item's own JSON has `price` before `sku`, writing that item as-is puts `price` first in the CSV too — rebuild each row as `{ sku: ..., qty: ..., price: ... }` before writing, so the column order is yours, not the input's.

`read(csv, "application/csv")` gets you back an array of objects, but every field on them is a String, `qty` and `price` included — the numbers you wrote in are not the numbers you read back. Coerce with `as Number` again before multiplying.

explanation.approach: `write(value, mime)` is a function like any other: it does not print, it returns a String holding the rendered CSV, ready to sit inside a field of a JSON object the same as a number or another string would. The first surprise is that this is exactly right — the CSV shows up in the output as one long string with `\r\n` escapes in it rather than looking like a table, because a JSON string cannot contain a literal newline. The second surprise is where the column order comes from: `write` uses the field order of the objects it is given, not any order implied by the question, so an item that arrives with `price` before `sku` writes `price` first unless each row is rebuilt with the field order fixed by hand before writing. The third is that `read` undoes the format but not the types — everything that comes back out of a CSV is a String, including the numbers, so they need `as Number` again before they can be multiplied.

snippets.label: write returns a String; embedded, it is an escaped blob
snippets.note: typeOf confirms it is just a String. Sitting inside the envelope it shows up as `\r\n`, not real line breaks — that is what a JSON string does to any text with newlines in it, and it is exactly what should happen here.

snippets.label: column order follows the object's own field order, not the question's
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
write([{price: 3, sku: "F6", qty: 4}], "application/csv")
snippets.note: This row's own JSON lists price, then sku, then qty, and the CSV header comes out in that same order — price first. Nothing about `write` knows the columns are supposed to read sku, qty, price.

snippets.label: the fix is rebuilding the row before writing it
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
var raw = {price: 3, sku: "F6", qty: 4}
---
write([{ sku: raw.sku, qty: raw.qty, price: raw.price }], "application/csv")
snippets.note: Same data, rebuilt as `{ sku, qty, price }` first. The column order is now the one the object literal states, not whatever order the source happened to arrive in.

snippets.label: read reverses the format but not the types
snippets.note: The 2 and the 9.5 went in as Numbers and came back as the Strings "2" and "9.5". read does not remember what the values were before write turned them into text.

snippets.label: the total needs those fields coerced back to Number
snippets.note: Without `as Number` on both fields, this multiplies Strings that only look numeric, which is not the computation the question asks for even on the rows where it happens not to throw.

title: Run a list of pricing rules through a pipeline
prompt:
Each order has a `base` price and a `rules` array. Each rule is `{ op, amount }`, where `op` is `"add"`, `"mul"`, or `"sub"`. Starting from `base`, apply the rules **in the order given** — an `"add"` adds `amount`, `"mul"` multiplies by `amount`, `"sub"` subtracts `amount`. An `op` that is none of those three leaves the running total unchanged.

Return an array of `{ id, total }`. An order with no rules keeps its `base` as `total`.
hints: A rule is naturally a one-argument function from price to price: give the operation and amount, get back a function that does that step. That is partial application — a function returning a function.

`then` composes a value with a callback — `then(x, f)` is `f(x)`. Fold the rules array into a chain of these with `reduce`, seeding the accumulator with `base` the way `[] reduce ((i, acc = 0) -> acc + i)` seeds it with `0`.

The natural first draft, `acc then applyOp(r.op, r.amount)`, does not compile — the infix form of `then` only accepts a literal lambda on its right, not a call to a named function. Write it as `then(acc, applyOp(r.op, r.amount))` instead, and never as separate running totals grouped by operation: `add`s and `mul`s do not commute, so grouping them loses the order the rules were given in.

explanation.approach: A rule is a step in a pipeline, and the natural way to represent a step is a one-argument function: give `applyOp` the operation and amount, and it hands back a function from price to price without running it yet — that is partial application. `then` is DataWeave's way to compose a value with a callback: `then(x, f)` is exactly `f(x)`, and folding the rules array with `reduce`, calling `then` once per rule, builds the pipeline in the order the rules appear. The trap is that `then` has two faces. Its function-call form, `then(acc, applyOp(...))`, accepts any callback, including one that came from calling a named function. Its infix form, `acc then applyOp(...)`, does not — it only works when the right-hand side is a lambda written out inline, and fails the moment it is a call to a `fun`, whether or not that call still takes more arguments. The two forms are not interchangeable despite looking like the same operation written two ways.

snippets.label: Partial application: a function that returns a function
snippets.note: applyOp("add", 5) does not compute a number — it returns a Function, still waiting for `x`. Calling that result with (10) is what actually runs the addition.

snippets.label: then's function-call form composes it
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
fun applyOp(op: String, amount: Number) = (x: Number) -> op match {
  case "add" -> x + amount
  case "mul" -> x * amount
  else -> x
}
---
then(10, applyOp("add", 5))
snippets.note: then(10, applyOp("add", 5)) is then(10, f) where f is the function from the previous snippet — it runs f(10) and gets 15. This is the form the pipeline is built from.

snippets.label: The infix spelling of the exact same thing does not compile
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
fun applyOp(op: String, amount: Number) = (x: Number) -> op match {
  case "add" -> x + amount
  case "mul" -> x * amount
  else -> x
}
---
10 then applyOp("add", 5)
snippets.note: Same values, same callback, written as `10 then applyOp("add", 5)` instead of `then(10, applyOp("add", 5))`. It fails with UnsupportedTypeCoercionException: Cannot coerce Function to String. Infix `then` does not accept a callback produced by calling a named function — bare or applied, with or without type annotations, it fails the same way. This is why the pipeline has to be built with the function-call form, not the infix one.

snippets.label: Infix then is fine with a lambda written out inline
snippets.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
10 then ((x) -> x + 5)
snippets.note: The only difference from the previous snippet is that the callback here is a lambda literal instead of a call to `applyOp`. It compiles and runs. `then` itself is not broken — only its infix form's tolerance for where the callback comes from is limited.

snippets.label: Order changes the answer, which is why grouping by operation is wrong
snippets.note: Same two rules, opposite order, different totals — 220 against 210. An approach that sums all the adds and multiplies by all the muls as separate batches cannot tell these two apart, because it throws away the order the rules came in.

title: Classify raw events by their shape
prompt:
A raw event feed mixes several shapes with no discriminator field to tell them apart — only the fields present say what an event is.

Declare a `ClickEvent` type with `x` and `y`, both Numbers, and a `KeyEvent` type with `key`, a String. For each event, return `{ id, type }`, where `type` is `"Click"` if it matches `ClickEvent`, `"Key"` if it matches `KeyEvent`, or `"Unknown"` otherwise. An event can only be classified by checking it against the declared types with `is` — there is no field named `type` on the input to read.

If an event matches both shapes at once, classify it as `"Click"`.
hints: `type Name = { ... }` declares a shape, and `value is Name` checks a value against it structurally — you never build an instance of the type, you only test against it.

title: Rename every key, everywhere, at any depth
prompt:
You are given JSON of unknown shape — objects nested inside arrays nested inside objects, to any depth. Every key that uses `snake_case` has to come out `camelCase`, no matter how deep it sits.

hints: You don't know the depth or the shape ahead of time, so this can't be a fixed chain of selectors — it needs something that looks at whatever it's handed, and calls itself again on whatever's inside.

  var parts = s splitBy "_"
  var rest = parts[1 to -1] default []
  ---
  parts[0] ++ ((rest map ((w) -> upper(w[0] default "") ++ (w[1 to -1] default ""))) joinBy "")
}
fun rewrite(v) = v match {
  case o is Object -> o mapObject ((val, key) -> { (camelKey(key)): rewrite(val) })
  case a is Array -> a map rewrite($)
  else -> v
}
---

  ???

A `match` with `case n is Number` and `case o is Object` gives you the two shapes. Inside the Object case, the two sides (`o.l` and `o.r`) have to be run back through the same evaluation before you apply the operator to them — combining them first and checking their type second is the bug that only shows up once a side is itself a node.

Splitting the work into two functions — one that picks the shape, one that applies the operator once both sides are already numbers — is fine, and they can call each other (`eval` calls a helper for the Object case, and that helper calls `eval` again on `o.l` and `o.r`) with no return-type annotation on either.   case "-" -> eval(o.l) - eval(o.r)
  case "*" -> eval(o.l) * eval(o.r)
  case "/" -> eval(o.l) / eval(o.r)
}
---
eval(payload)

Splitting that into two functions — `eval` for the shape test, `evalNode` for applying the operator once both sides are already evaluated — makes them mutually recursive (`eval` calls `evalNode`, `evalNode` calls `eval`), and neither needs a return-type annotation to compile. title: Validate a record against a schema given as data
prompt:
The payload is `{ schema, record }`. `schema` is an object mapping field names to a rule shaped like `{ kind, required }`, where `kind` is one of `"String"`, `"Number"`, `"Boolean"`, `"Object"`, `"Array"`, and `required` is `true` or `false`.

When `kind` is `"Object"`, the rule also has `fields` — another schema of the same shape, describing `record`'s nested value for that field. When `kind` is `"Array"`, the rule also has `itemKind` — one of the scalar kinds, which every element of the array must match.

Return an array of every violation found anywhere in `record`, as strings, in the form `<path> is required` or `<path> must be a <Kind>`, using a dotted path such as `user.address.city` and a bracketed index such as `tags[1]` for array elements. A field that is missing is only a violation when its rule says it is required. Find every violation, not just the first one for a field and not just the first field with a problem — a record with three things wrong reports all three.

hints: For each field the schema mentions, look up the matching value in the record and ask the same two questions: is it missing when it shouldn't be, and if it's present, does it have the shape the rule describes. That question is identical at every depth — the only thing that changes going into a nested Object field is which schema and which value you're asking it about.

Each field resolves to its own small array of errors — often empty. The overall answer is every one of those little arrays, flattened into one, which is a job for `pluck` (it hands you the rule and the field name for every entry) rather than a variable you keep appending to as you go.

`match` on `rule.kind` picks the check. `"Object"` and `"Array"` are not leaves: for `"Object"`, call the validator again on `rule.fields` and the nested value, with the path extended by the field's name; for `"Array"`, check `rule.itemKind` against every element and collect all of their errors. A version that only confirms the value IS an Object, or IS an Array, without going one level further in, matches a flat schema exactly and reports nothing at all for anything nested inside one.

explanation.approach: Each field in the schema resolves to its own small array of errors — empty when that field is fine — and the overall result is every one of those arrays flattened together, so nothing needs a running total that grows as the walk proceeds. `pluck` supplies the `(rule, field)` pairs; for each one, `record[field]` is looked up and tested for missing-when-required, then, if it is present, matched against `rule.kind`. Three of the five kinds are leaves and get checked with `is` directly. The other two are not: `"Object"` means there is a nested schema (`rule.fields`) and a nested value, and `validate` is called again on exactly those, with the path extended by the field's own name; `"Array"` means every element gets checked against `rule.itemKind` and all of those results get flattened in too. The near-miss stops at confirming the field's own container type and never goes back inside it — which behaves identically to the real thing on a schema that happens not to nest, and silently drops every violation that lives one level deeper.
